Title: Research through Design (RtD)
Description: Explored generative design spaces and tangible user interactions through physical prototyping and research-through-design methodology.
longDescription: During my MSc in Integrated Product Design at TU Delft, I worked with research through design as a methodology — using making as a way of asking questions rather than simply presenting answers. The project involved creating physical prototypes as tools for exploring how people relate to objects and interactions. Each iteration was not just a step toward a final product but a deliberate act of inquiry, generating insights that could not have been reached through analysis alone. This approach taught me to hold design and research in parallel: to be rigorous about what a prototype reveals, and open-ended about what it means. It sits at the core of how I now approach early-stage product development.

Title: Klimmende Stapelaar
Description: Designed, calculated, and built a climbing stacker mechanism as part of the Mechanical Engineering BSc at TU Delft — translating kinematic requirements into a working physical prototype.
longDescription: The Klimmende Stapelaar (climbing stacker) was a mechanical engineering project in which the goal was to design a mechanism capable of stacking objects by climbing along a vertical structure. Starting from a kinematic brief, I worked through the full mechanical development cycle: defining the motion requirements, selecting a suitable mechanism topology, dimensioning components through stress and stiffness calculations, producing detailed CAD models, and finally fabricating and testing a physical prototype. The challenge was not just in getting the kinematics right, but in translating a theoretical mechanism into something that could actually be built and would hold together under load. The project gave me direct experience of the gap between a design on paper and a working physical system — and of the problem-solving required to close it. It is a project I value for showing what it takes to go from a mechanical concept all the way to a functioning prototype.

Title: Custom Mini Vehicle
Description: Designed and fabricated a miniature vehicle prototype from scratch — engineering the chassis
Image: and steering for stability and controlled motion.
column10: This project involved designing and building a small vehicle from the ground up. Rather than starting from a kit or standard platform, I developed the mechanical layout from scratch: chassis geometry, drivetrain gearing, and steering linkage were all designed with the constraints of a miniature vehicle in mind. A key focus was making the different systems work together within a compact envelope — the gearing had to deliver enough torque for clean acceleration while the chassis needed to be stiff enough to keep the steering predictable. The fabrication process meant working closely with what was actually buildable, often iterating on parts that worked in CAD but needed adjustment once assembled. The result was a functional prototype that demonstrated the full chain from mechanical concept to physical vehicle — and gave me a thorough understanding of how chassis, drivetrain, and steering interact in practice.

Title: Direct Air Carbon Capture Paper
Description: Investigated the thermodynamic feasibility of a mechanical direct air capture system, modelling energy demands and assessing scalability.
longDescription: This paper explored direct air capture (DAC) of CO₂ from an engineering perspective. The starting point was a proposed mechanical DAC system, and the task was to assess whether it could work at meaningful scale given realistic thermodynamic constraints. I worked through the physics of the capture process, modelled the energy requirements at different scales, and evaluated what the numbers meant for the practical feasibility of the approach. The work was analytical rather than experimental — the value lay in applying thermodynamic reasoning to a real-world problem and communicating the conclusions clearly. It sharpened my ability to frame an engineering question, work through it systematically, and present a technically grounded argument. For my portfolio, it demonstrates that my engineering thinking extends beyond physical design into research, modelling, and technical communication.

Title: Mini CNC Machine
Description: Designed and assembled a compact, functional 3-axis CNC machine — integrating structural design, motion control, and mechatronics into a working desktop system.
longDescription: Building a desktop CNC machine required thinking about mechanical design and motion systems at the same time. The machine needed a rigid frame, well-supported linear guides on each axis, and stepper-motor-driven motion that could be controlled precisely enough to cut useful parts. I designed the structure and axis layout in CAD, selected and integrated the linear guides and drive components, fabricated and assembled the frame, and configured the motion control system. Getting it to work meant iterating on both the mechanical design and the electronics — small issues in rigidity or alignment had a direct effect on cutting quality. The project is a good example of the kind of hands-on, integrated engineering I find most satisfying: where structural design, kinematics, and electronics all have to come together in a single working system.

Title: Baxter Roll
Description: Developed a product concept through research, mechanical design, prototyping, and iteration — with equal attention to function and how the product should feel to use.
longDescription: Baxter Roll was a full product development project in which I moved from early research through concept development to a detailed mechanical prototype. The goal was not just to arrive at something that worked mechanically, but to develop a product whose feel of use was considered from the start. This meant thinking about ergonomics, material character, and interaction quality alongside structural requirements. The process involved several prototype iterations — each one testing a different set of assumptions and feeding back into the design. SolidWorks was used for detailed 3D modelling and to work through component relationships before committing to physical builds. The project represents the kind of work that sits at the intersection of engineering and product design: technically grounded, but always with the user's experience as the frame of reference.

Title: Hyperion Lyceum
Description: Completed VWO at Hyperion Lyceum in Amsterdam, with a strong foundation in mathematics, natural sciences, and analytical reasoning as preparation for TU Delft.
longDescription: Before starting at TU Delft, I completed VWO at Hyperion Lyceum in Amsterdam. The curriculum had a strong emphasis on mathematics and the natural sciences — physics, chemistry, and biology — alongside subjects that required analytical thinking and clear argumentation. This period gave me a solid grounding in the kind of quantitative reasoning that underpins engineering, and an early appreciation for working through complex problems systematically. The transition from secondary school to Mechanical Engineering at Delft felt like a natural continuation of that direction.

Title: IDE Business Fair
Short description: Chair, IDE Business Fair organising committee
Description: As chair of the organising committee, led the planning and delivery of the TU Delft IDE Business Fair (March 2026) — connecting design students with companies through exhibitions, workshops, and design cases.
longDescription: The IDE Business Fair is an annual event at TU Delft's Industrial Design Engineering faculty that brings together design students and companies. As chair of the organising committee, I was responsible for the overall coordination of the 2026 edition: managing the committee, approaching and acquiring participating companies, and ensuring the event delivered value for both students and company partners. This meant balancing practical logistics with outreach and relationship-building — explaining the fair's format to company contacts, discussing how they might engage (through stands, workshops, design cases, or recruitment activities), and working to match what companies were looking for with what students needed. Beyond the event itself, it was an exercise in taking responsibility for a complex, multi-stakeholder project and seeing it through from planning to delivery.

Title: Offshore Workability Analysis
Description: At Ampelmann, I assess whether planned motion-compensated walk-to-work operations are viable — combining weather data, vessel specifications, and operational limits into structured feasibility reports.
longDescription: At Ampelmann, my work centres on offshore workability analysis for motion-compensated walk-to-work systems. These systems allow personnel to transfer between vessels and offshore structures in sea conditions that would otherwise prevent safe access. The core question in each analysis is whether a planned operation is feasible given the expected environmental conditions, the vessel involved, and the limits of the equipment. This means working with wave and weather data, understanding vessel motion behaviour, applying operational criteria, and presenting the conclusions in a form that is useful for planning and decision-making. The work sits at the boundary between engineering analysis and practical operations support. It has given me experience of working in a professional engineering environment, handling real data, and communicating technical results to people who use them to make decisions offshore. It also demonstrates that my engineering background extends into applied analysis and technical reporting, not only physical design.

Title: High School STEM Tutoring
Description: Provided one-on-one tutoring and exam preparation for secondary school students in mathematics, physics, and chemistry — finding the explanation that worked for each student.
longDescription: As a tutor, I worked one-on-one with secondary school students preparing for mathematics, physics, and chemistry examinations. The job was essentially about communication: understanding where a student was getting stuck, finding a different way in, and helping them build a mental model they could actually use. Technical subjects often look impenetrable from the outside, but they usually have a logic that becomes clear once the right angle is found. Part of what I enjoy about tutoring is the problem-solving aspect — not the subject matter itself, but the puzzle of how to explain something in a way that connects. This experience has reinforced how I think about communicating technical ideas more broadly: the goal is always clarity and usefulness for the person on the other end, not completeness for its own sake.

Title: Platenmeubel (Vinyl Cabinet)
Description: Designed and hand-built a wooden cabinet for vinyl records and turntable — a project in furniture design, joinery, and careful attention to material and proportion.
Image: WhatsApp Image 2026-09-25 at 11.53.33.jpeg, WhatsApp Image 2026-09-25 at 11.53.34.jpeg, WhatsApp Image 2026-09-25 at 11.58.42.jpeg, WhatsApp Image 2026-09-25 at 11.58.44.jpeg
longDescription: The Platenmeubel started as a practical need — somewhere to put a turntable and store records — and became a full furniture design and build project. I drew up the design in AutoCAD, working through the proportions, the internal layout for record storage, and the details of how the pieces would join. The material is warm-toned wood, chosen for its visual character as much as its workability. The build involved hand and machine joinery, surface finishing, and fitting everything together so the piece felt considered rather than assembled. I added ribbed panels and indirect lighting as deliberate design features, to give the cabinet its own presence in a room. This project is personal, but it reflects the same thinking I bring to product design work: attention to proportion, material honesty, and the difference between something that functions and something that also feels right to live with.

Title: Ergonomic Laptop Stand
Description: Designed and fabricated a laptop stand optimised for posture, passive airflow, and everyday desk aesthetics — a small exercise in taking a simple problem seriously.
longDescription: The laptop stand is a small project, but it is a useful one for my portfolio because it shows how I approach even simple design problems. The brief I set myself was straightforward: raise the screen to a more comfortable viewing angle, allow air to circulate under the laptop, and make something that belongs on a clean desk rather than looking like an afterthought. This meant thinking about the geometry of the stand in relation to typical sitting posture, the structural requirements for carrying a laptop's weight without flex, and the visual character of the object. The result is a stand that does its job quietly — which is what a good workstation accessory should do. It is a project that demonstrates that the same design principles apply at every scale: define the problem carefully, consider the constraints, and make something that works well and looks considered.

Title: Photography
Short description: Stills shaped by light, texture, and overlooked moments.
Description: Photographing with whatever is to hand — looking for the in-between moments that do not ask to be noticed, led by atmosphere, composition, and natural light.
longDescription: Photography, for me, is a practice in paying attention. I am drawn to natural light, material textures, and the kind of moments that do not announce themselves — a certain quality of shadow, an unexpected juxtaposition, something that would be easy to walk past. I work with whatever camera is available and try not to over-engineer the image. The interest is in seeing clearly, not in production value. I include photography in my portfolio not as a technical design project but as evidence of a visual sensibility that feeds into everything else I do. How you frame something, what you decide to include and exclude, and what you are drawn to notice — these habits of attention transfer directly into product design, communication, and research.

Title: Writing & Production
Short description: Instrumental music focused on texture and space.
Description: Writing and producing mostly instrumental music — interested in texture, space, and the way an idea develops and resolves over time.
longDescription: I write and produce mostly instrumental music. My interest is in how sounds relate to one another over time — the texture of a piece, the space between things, and the way tension builds and resolves. I work with both recorded and synthesised material, and I spend a lot of time on arrangement: figuring out which elements need to be present and which ones should be absent. The process is iterative in the same way that physical design work is iterative — you make something, listen back, understand what it is actually doing rather than what you intended, and adjust. Music sits outside my engineering work, but the habits it requires — listening carefully, being willing to discard what does not serve the whole, and caring about subtle differences — are ones I value in any creative or technical context.

Title: EasyTabMaker
Description: Built easytabmaker.com — a free, clean guitar tab editor with no intrusive ads, shareable tabs, and user accounts.
longDescription: I started EasyTabMaker because I could not find a free guitar tab editor that felt good to use. The existing tools were either cluttered with advertising, unnecessarily complex, or missing basic features. Rather than continue working around them, I decided to build my own. The result is a web application with a clean, focused interface for writing guitar tabs, plus user accounts that allow tabs to be saved, edited, and shared. Building it involved working through the full product stack: designing the interface, writing the front-end, handling data persistence and accounts on the back end, and thinking carefully about how the editing interaction should feel. The project connects two of my interests — music and building useful tools — and gave me a practical opportunity to apply UX thinking to something I actually needed. The current version is live at easytabmaker.com.
